title: Concept-Guided Spatial Regularization for World Models in Atari Pong
hook: Five world-model RL agents can master Atari Pong on paper — but freeze their world models and watch closely: the ball vanishes, bounces wrong, or phases through the paddle.
key_points: Audited 5 world-model RL agents (DreamerV3, DIAMOND, TWISTER, Simulus, STORM) on Atari Pong by freezing the learned world model and inspecting its rollouts directly.
All five show clear rollout failures: ball disappearance, wrong ball motion, invalid ball-paddle interactions.
Training a fresh policy entirely inside a frozen world model badly underperforms the original agent — DreamerV3's return drops from -5.5 to -20.9, near the worst possible score.

Proposes Concept-Guided Spatial Regularization (CGSReg): an auxiliary reconstruction loss on segmented concept regions (like the ball) that improves rollouts and zero-shot policy transfer for 3 of the 5 models.
content_html: World models are usually judged indirectly, by how well the reinforcement-learning agent built on top of them plays the game. This paper instead freezes five well-known world-model agents — DreamerV3, DIAMOND, TWISTER, Simulus, and STORM — after reproducing their reported Atari Pong performance, and studies the world models on their own.
extra_html:
Yukuan Lu and colleagues run two tests. First, a policy trained separately from each agent's own training pipeline is dropped into the frozen world model, and the resulting imagined video is inspected frame by frame: every single model shows failures like the ball vanishing, moving incorrectly, or passing through the paddle. Second, a harsher test — training a brand-new policy entirely inside the frozen world model, then evaluating it back in the real game — reveals how costly those glitches are: DreamerV3's return falls from -5.5 to -20.9, barely above the worst possible score in Pong.

The authors' hypothesis is that these models simply don't represent task-critical objects, like the ball, precisely enough. Their fix, Concept-Guided Spatial Regularization (CGSReg), adds a reconstruction loss focused on segmented concept regions during training. It measurably improves rollout quality and zero-shot policy transfer for three of the five models (DreamerV3, DIAMOND, TWISTER), but its effect is inconsistent on the rest — evidence that concept modeling is one bottleneck among several. Source: arXiv, arxiv.org/abs/2607.15142.

flashcards.prompt: How did the authors evaluate world models in isolation, rather than as part of a full RL agent?
flashcards.back_html: They froze each trained world model and ran a separately-trained policy inside it (closed-loop rollouts), then inspected the generated video for visual and dynamical errors.

flashcards.prompt: What happened when a new policy was trained entirely inside DreamerV3's frozen world model, then tested in the real Pong environment?

choices.text: Mean return collapsed from -5.5 to -20.9, near the worst possible Pong score
It matched the performance of the original DreamerV3 agent
It outperformed the original agent by a wide margin
The world model refused to produce any rollout

flashcards.explanation_html: This zero-shot pixel-space MBRL test exposed how much the world model's own imagined dynamics diverge from reality once a policy has to rely on them alone.

flashcards.back_html: An auxiliary pixel-reconstruction loss applied specifically to segmented task-critical regions (like the ball in Pong), meant to force the world model to represent them more reliably.

flashcards.prompt: Did CGSReg fix the world-model failures across all five agents tested?

choices.text: No — it improved rollouts and zero-shot MBRL for DreamerV3, DIAMOND, and TWISTER, but effects varied on the rest
Yes, it fully eliminated rollout errors in all five agents
No, it made every model's rollouts worse

flashcards.explanation_html: The authors are explicit that CGSReg helps but doesn't fix everything, showing insufficient concept modeling is only part of what limits these world models.
